request.job_description: We are hiring an Applied AI Engineer to build and ship LLM-powered features for our customer support product. You will design retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines, build evaluation harnesses to measure quality and regressions, and productionize services in Python. You will work with product and design to translate ambiguous user problems into measurable AI features, and own latency, cost and quality in production. Requirements: 3+ years of software engineering experience, hands-on experience shipping LLM features, strong Python, and a rigorous approach to evaluation.

transcript.question: Walk me through a RAG system you built end to end. What were the key design decisions?
transcript.answer: I built a support-answer assistant over about 40,000 help-center articles and resolved-ticket summaries. I started with fixed 512-token chunks and plain dense retrieval, and recall@5 on our labelled set was around 0.71. Chunking by document structure (headings and sections) with a 15 percent overlap raised it to 0.78. Adding BM25 hybrid retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion got to 0.86, and a cross-encoder reranker on the top 30 candidates pushed it to 0.91. I kept the reranker because it added about 120 ms at p50, which fit our budget. I also added metadata filters on product and plan tier, which removed a class of wrong-product answers that had been about 6 percent of failures.

transcript.question: How did you evaluate that system, both offline and in production?
transcript.answer: Offline, I built a golden set of 400 questions sampled from real tickets, stratified by topic, with labelled relevant documents and reference answers. I measured retrieval with recall@k and MRR, and for generation I used an LLM judge scoring faithfulness and answer correctness. I calibrated the judge against 150 human-labelled examples and got about 0.82 agreement, then fixed a bias where it preferred longer answers by adding a length-controlled rubric. It ran in CI on every prompt or retriever change and blocked merges if faithfulness dropped more than 2 points. In production, I tracked thumbs up/down, escalation-to-human rate and sampled 50 conversations a week for manual review. Escalation rate dropped from 38 to 27 percent after launch.

transcript.question: Tell me about a production incident or quality regression with an LLM feature and how you handled it.
transcript.answer: After a provider model version update, our faithfulness score on the nightly eval dropped from 0.93 to 0.86 even though we hadn't changed anything. I had pinned the model version for the main path but a fallback path used the alias, so it silently switched. I traced it by diffing outputs on the golden set and found the new version was more verbose and added unsupported details. I pinned the version on all paths, tightened the prompt to say answer only from provided context, and added an alert on nightly eval drops over 3 points. Recovery took about a day, and I wrote a postmortem and added a rule that every model call must specify a pinned version, enforced by a lint check.

transcript.question: How do you think about cost and latency trade-offs when shipping an LLM feature?
transcript.answer: I start with a budget: for support chat we wanted p95 under 4 seconds to first useful token and under 2 cents per conversation. We streamed responses so perceived latency was about 900 ms. I routed simple intent questions, about 45 percent of traffic, to a smaller model and kept the larger one for complex queries, using a classifier with a confidence threshold. That cut cost per conversation by roughly 40 percent, with a 1 point quality drop on our eval that we judged acceptable. We also cached embeddings and added a semantic cache for frequent questions, which hit about 12 percent of the time. I'd revisit the routing threshold monthly, because the quality gap between models changes.

transcript.question: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a product partner about launching an AI feature.
transcript.answer: A product manager wanted to launch an auto-reply feature that sent answers directly to customers, with a deadline in two weeks. Our eval showed 92 percent correctness, but the 8 percent errors included billing questions where a wrong answer is costly. I broke down errors by category and showed that billing and refunds accounted for most of the severe ones. I proposed launching auto-reply for low-risk categories and a draft-for-agent mode for billing, with a plan to expand once severe error rate was under 1 percent. The PM agreed, we hit the date with a narrower scope, and we expanded to billing six weeks later after improving retrieval on policy documents.
